source_descriptions.description:
The registration page is the form opened by the unique link named “Create an account” from the sign-in page. The form contains exactly one textbox labeled “Username”, one textbox labeled “Email”, one password input labeled “Password”, one password input labeled “Confirm password”, one initially unchecked checkbox named “Agree to the terms”, and one enabled button named “Create account”. The username and email identify the account, while passwords must not be echoed on the page. This product directly marks the email of a successfully registered account as verified and does not provide a subsequent email-verification page. The visitor enters a unique username, email, password, and matching confirmation, checks “Agree to the terms”, and activates “Create account”. The username must consist of 1 to 39 lowercase ASCII letters, digits, or single hyphens (`-`) and must not begin or end with a hyphen; after trimming leading and trailing whitespace, the email must contain exactly one `@`, be no longer than 254 characters, and have at least one dot and non-empty domain labels after the `@`; the password must contain 12 to 128 characters, include at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter, one digit, and one non-alphanumeric special character, and contain no whitespace characters. The system stores a sign-in-capable account together with its verified-email status and enters the sign-in page; if the username or email conflicts, any field is missing, the email format is invalid, the terms are not accepted, the password is noncompliant, or the confirmation does not match, the system retains the username and email input, displays an itemized message beside the corresponding field, and does not create an account. The corresponding visible field message contains “Username already exists”, “Username format is invalid”, “Email format is invalid”, “Password requirements are not satisfied”, or “Agree to terms is required”, as applicable. Visitors can use this capability on the account-access page. The system validates input rules, displays field errors, and prevents duplicate accounts; on success, it directly creates an available account. Submitting several invalid fields together must show the username, email, password, and missing-terms messages together, rather than revealing only one error per submission; the submit button remains actionable so these messages can be read. For example, a username beginning with a hyphen, email “not-an-email”, password “short”, confirmation “different”, and unchecked terms produce these field errors and preserve the attempted username. A duplicate username paired with a different unused email displays “Username already exists” and retains both attempted values. A successful registration accepts a unique username such as “pw-user-<unique suffix>”, its “@example.test” email, and password “Valid-password-123!”; the sign-in form is immediately available, accepts that email, and the resulting signed-in username remains visible after reload.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-up.png)

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-1-1-1 (Register a New GitHub Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The sign-in page is the form on the account-access page containing “Username or email”, “Password”, and “Sign in”. A “session” is the current-browser login record saved after successful account authentication, represented in the frontend by the upper-right account menu and access to protected pages. The visitor enters a username or email and a password and submits the form. The system looks up the account and validates its credentials and availability status; if authentication fails due to an unknown username/email, incorrect password, or unavailable account, the system displays exactly the same generic failure message “Invalid credentials”, does not disclose whether the account exists or which credential was wrong, and does not create a session. After successful authentication, the system stores a session with a unique session identifier, account identifier, and active status, then redirects to the workspace accessible to that user; the session remains valid after refreshing or reopening the workspace, and subsequent protected organization, repository, and work-item requests must use this session to determine the current user.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-sign-in.png)

From the repository's “Settings” link, open the “Manage access” link and activate “Add people or teams”. The picker presents a textbox “Search”, a matching selectable team option whose name contains the team name, a combobox “Role” with clickable role options including “Write”, and an “Add” button. While the picker is active, hide the opening Add people or teams button from the active view so the submit action is unambiguous. After saving, the authorization list visibly shows the exact team name and Write role and retains the team after reload. Existing grants appear as rows whose accessible names include the subject name; each row contains a native select labeled “Role” and a “Save” button. Selecting the option labeled “Read” and saving replaces Write; after reload exactly one row for the team remains and contains Read. The creation scenario supplies a repository Admin and an organization team not yet granted access; the replacement scenario supplies a separate repository/team with an existing Write grant. An organization Owner or repository Admin may grant a repository role of Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, or Admin to a current organization member or team. In the access-subject picker, matching member or team options update as the administrator types; pressing Enter or activating a separate search button is not required before selecting an option. A private repository is accessible only to an organization Owner, a member with a direct repository role, or a direct member of a team that has a repository role; an ordinary organization Member has no default private-repository access. For a given subject and repository, only one direct role grant is stored — saving the same role again does not create a second record, and changing the role replaces the original role. An account's effective repository role is the highest among Admin from Owner status and all still-valid direct grants and team grants; team hierarchy does not propagate membership or authorization. The system stores the authorization subject, repository, role, grantor, and timestamp and authorizes operations according to the ROOT role matrix; unauthorized accounts cannot see private repositories. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-2-1-2 (Create an Organization After Authentication) and REQ-2-2-1 (Create an Organization Team); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

The repository overview identifies the repository in a heading containing “owner/repository name”, displays a visible “Public” marker for a public repository, and provides a navigation link “Code”. This link is distinct from the clone-menu Code button. A seeded public repository with its matching name and stable address is readable without sign-in and retains the same heading after reload. Visitors or authorized users can open a repository overview to confirm repository identity, visibility, description, primary metadata, and available content. The overview provides the primary entry points for browsing files, viewing repository context, and beginning collaboration.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-repository-overview.png)

The user opens the branch selector, enters a new branch name, confirms the displayed base branch or commit, and clicks “Create branch: <name>”. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-1 (Browse Repository Files and Directories) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. The file editor is the form opened from Edit or Add file on the Code page; the user edits file content at a path on the current branch and submits it. Only Write, Maintain, Admin, or organization Owner may submit; Read and Triage may only view. A single submission stores the file-path and content change, commit message, author, parent commit, and target branch as one indivisible record and moves the target branch to point to that new commit. A new or renamed file path must not be empty, must not begin with `/`, must not contain a `..` path segment, and must not conflict with an existing file or directory on the current branch; the commit message must contain 1–72 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace. If the path conflicts, content validation fails, the commit message is noncompliant, the branch is protected, or persistence fails, the page displays the reason and does not change the file, branch head, or commit history. An invalid path displays “Invalid file path”, and an empty commit message displays “Commit message is required”. From the writable Code page, the unique “Add file” button opens the “Create new file” menuitem. The editor has a field labeled “File name”, a textbox named “File contents”, an initially empty field labeled “Commit message”, and a “Commit changes” button. Creating a unique file such as `pw-file-<unique suffix>.md` with nonempty text and a message such as `Add <file name>` immediately opens a view displaying the exact saved content. Its “Commits” link opens history displaying the exact submitted message. Submitting `../invalid.md` with content `must not be saved` and no commit message reports the invalid path and/or required message and changes neither files nor history. The example content is ordinary text, not a forbidden content value by itself; rejection follows from the invalid path or missing message.

![image](reference/github-web-file-editor.png)

The valid comparison page is directly accessible to the signed-in contributor. Its Create pull request button opens a form with a field labeled Title, an optional Description field, and a single Create pull request submit button; the comparison-page action is no longer a competing active button. Successful submission shows the entered title as the exact PR heading and visible Open status, and the title survives reload. A title containing only spaces is rejected with Title is required and creates no PR. A user with Write, Maintain, or Admin clicks “Create pull request” on a valid comparison-results page, enters a title containing 1–256 non-empty characters after trimming leading and trailing whitespace and an optional description of at most 65536 characters, confirms distinct base/compare branches with differences, and clicks “Create pull request”. The system atomically creates an Open PR, stores a unique repository-scoped number, source/target branches, current compare commit, current base commit, title, description, author, creation time, and activity record, and redirects to the detail page; if there is no difference, the branches are the same, a Draft or Open PR with the same source/target pair already exists, the title is empty or overlong, the user lacks permission, or submission fails, no record is created. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-2-2 (Compare Branches Before Opening a Pull Request); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.

This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-4-3-1 (List and Switch Repository Branches) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes. A “branch protection rule” is a persistent merge restriction bound to one exact branch name, displayed in the frontend under Settings → Branches, with the backend storing the branch name and rule toggles. This product supports only two independently selectable requirements: “at least 1 valid Approve from someone other than the PR author” and “required check `test` is success”. For a given reviewer on the same current compare commit, only the reviewer's latest decision among Comment, Approve, and Request changes counts. The system blocks direct writes to a protected branch and applies the rule during subsequent PR merging. The repository provides a Settings link followed by a Branches link. The rule form opens from the Add branch protection rule button and contains a field labeled Branch name pattern (an exact branch name, with no wildcard semantics), checkboxes named Require 1 approval and Require status check test, and a Create button; an existing rule uses Save changes. After saving and reloading, the branch name is visible verbatim with the summaries 1 approval and Require status check test. For a non-Admin, Add branch protection rule is absent, even if Settings or Branches remain accessible; rejecting a save alone is insufficient. On the PR detail page, the Checks area is available on arrival, displays test: pending initially, and offers the Admin a combobox named test status with a clickable option named success and a Save button. Saving displays test: success and identifies the setter and time, and reloading preserves the result for that compare commit. Seed data comprises a repository Admin and a readable non-Admin account, a dedicated repository and exact branch name with no existing rule before creation, and a separate Open PR targeting protected main with its current test check initially pending.

Screenshot reference:
![image](reference/github-branch-protection.png)

From the Files changed link, the reviewer activates the Review changes button to open one review form with an optional Summary field, radio controls named Comment, Approve, and Request changes, and a Submit review button. Selecting Approve and submitting without a summary is valid and displays Approved. Selecting Request changes with a summary displays Changes requested and that exact summary; the decision remains visible after reload. Seed data supplies a non-author Write reviewer and separate Open PRs for approval and request-changes submission, with no initial effective decision by that reviewer. A user who is not the PR author and has Write, Maintain, or Admin may submit Comment, Approve, or Request changes on an Open PR; the author and Draft PRs cannot submit reviews. The system stores the review decision, reviewer, current compare commit, optional explanation, and time; a new decision by the same reviewer replaces that reviewer's effective decision for the current commit while preserving the old record. Approve is valid only when the reviewer is not the author and the compare commit is still the same; Request changes blocks merging until that reviewer submits a new Comment or Approve for the current compare commit, or the compare branch receives a new commit that makes the old decision stale. This feature builds on the persisted objects, opened pages, or authenticated-session context provided by REQ-6-3-1 (View Pull Request Overview and Commits) and REQ-1-1-2 (Sign In with an Existing Account); it must reuse that context and keep pages and data consistent after the context changes.
